query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing the Cr content in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating increases the formation of a continuous, load‐bearing Cr-rich oxide during high-temperature sliding, which in turn mitigates adhesive wear and suppresses extensive microscopic plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Increase the Cr content by a controlled amount (e.g., adding ~5 at.% extra Cr relative to the baseline composition) while keeping other elements near their original levels.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., operating temperatures in the range of 500–800 °C under oxidative environment) with standard load and speed representative of the intended application.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Cr-rich oxide (likely Cr2O3) layer on the wear track during sliding.
generation.mechanism: The enriched Cr content promotes the rapid in-situ formation of a protective oxide film during sliding, which reduces metal-to-metal contact and friction. This oxide layer acts as a barrier that absorbs and redistributes shear stresses, thereby reducing adhesive wear and limiting the extent of microscopic plastic deformation in the coating.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified coating with increased Cr will exhibit reduced wear volume and a lower rate of microscopic plastic deformation compared to the baseline coating under identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu coating without any compositional adjustments.
generation.boundary: Predictions apply primarily during high-temperature, oxidative sliding regimes (approximately 500–800 °C) where in-situ oxidation is significant.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists in the precise kinetics and uniformity of oxide formation under varying sliding and environmental conditions, and the potential trade-offs (e.g., brittleness of the oxide layer) require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: the baseline equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu and the modified version with increased Cr content. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding tests in an oxidative atmosphere while maintaining constant load, speed, and environment. Use in situ or ex situ surface characterization techniques (e.g., SEM, XPS, TEM) to assess oxide layer formation and measure wear volume and microscopic deformation.
measurements: Wear volume and wear track depth measurements
Microstructural analysis of the oxide layer (thickness, continuity, phase identification)
Subsurface deformation patterns via cross-sectional microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified coating does not exhibit a significantly thicker, continuous, and protective Cr-rich oxide layer, or if wear volume and microscopic deformation are not reduced (or are worsened) compared to the baseline coating under high-temperature sliding, then the hypothesis that enhanced Cr-induced oxidation improves wear resistance would be falsified.
